data.title: Here's what happened next after previous times the S&P 500 losing streak reached six sessions
data.description:
By Steve Goldstein

Six-session losing runs are relatively rare, but they're not necessarily a bad sign of future returns.

For markets, it's been a week from hell - or, more accurately, the worst stretch for the S&P 500 since the "Liberation Day" tariffs of 2025 - but the history of six-session losing streaks actually points to some better news ahead.

First, inspired by a message from the OddStats social-media account, MarketWatch looked at the last nine times the S&P 500 had a six-day losing streak like this one where it's lost at least 5%.

The S&P 500 SPX was positive the next day, seven out of nine times, with a median return of 1.9%. (OddStats said it was up eight out of nine times; there may be confusion owing to the fact that one of the days occurred around the Thanksgiving holiday.)

The early action in S&P 500 futures (ES00) on Friday doesn't look great for this particular streak, however things can of course change; that same contract was higher in the premarket on Thursday before closing much lower.

Next comes this nugget from Ben Kizemchuk, a portfolio manager at Wellington-Altus, who looked more longer term.

He noted there have been just 57 occasions where the S&P 500 closed lower for six straight sessions since 1975.

The average path afterward was positive across every forward time horizon studied, with gains improving from +0.6% after one week to +2.6% after roughly six weeks. The index was higher 68%-70% of the time after 10-25 trading days.

MarketWatch crunched the numbers.

 
Horizon                  Sample Size  Mean Return (%)  Median Return (%)  Win Rate (%) 
Next_Day (1d)            57           0.42             0.34               64.9 
1_Week (5d)              57           0.6              0.7                66.7 
2_Weeks (10d)            57           0.56             0.68               57.9 
3_Weeks (15d)            57           1.02             1.51               68.4 
4_Weeks (20d)            57           2.28             2.16               68.4 
5_Weeks (25d)            57           2.36             2.19               70.2 
6_Weeks (30d)            57           2.65             1.23               66.7 
Source: Yfinance/Gemini

"While not a timing signal, the historical evidence suggests persistent selling pressure tends to be associated with seller exhaustion more often than the start of larger declines," said Kizemchuk.

-Steve Goldstein

data.title: Vedanta Aluminium Metal ramps up green energy use by 63% in FY26
data.description:
Vedanta Aluminium Metal Ltd (VAML) on Friday said it ramped up its use of green energy by 63 per cent in FY26 while continuing to improve energy efficiency across operations in Jharsuguda and Lanjigarh in Odisha and BALCO in Chhattisgarh.

During the year, the company consumed 2,562.81 million units of renewable energy and saved 635,757 MWh of energy through efficiency initiatives. As a result, VAML reduced its emissions intensity by 11.4 per cent compared to its FY21 baseline, bringing it down to 16.57 tonne of CO2 equivalent per tonne of aluminium.

The company also signed agreements for 493 MW round-the-clock renewable power as it works towards its 2030 clean power ambition.

It further said that nearly 16 million tonne of waste has been recycled and reused as VAML expands renewable energy use and lowers emissions.

"Aluminium has a vital role in India’s industrial growth and energy transition. Our responsibility is to increase supply while steadily improving how the metal is produced. The progress recorded this year reflects practical changes across our operations, from greater renewable energy use and energy efficiency to stronger recovery of water and materials," VAML CEO Rajesh Kumar said in a statement.

Vedanta Aluminium Metal Ltd is one of the world’s leading producers of aluminium. It caters to customers across more than 60 countries.

data.title: European shares on track for steepest weekly drop since March
data.description:
Key points:
  • STOXX 600 down 1.3%
  • Tech drops more than 3% as chip stocks sink
  • Vallourec slides after Q3 core profit decline

By Anjana Jayakrishnan Nair

European shares were headed for their steepest weekly decline since March on Friday, as investors unwound AI-linked bets after Anthropic's blockbuster market debut failed to revive confidence in the sector.

The pan-European STOXX 600 declined 1.3% to 630.22 points by 0926 GMT, on track for a weekly loss of more than 5%, its worst performance since the week ended March 6. The index was also trading at a six-week low.

Anthropic reached a roughly $2 trillion valuation in its Nasdaq debut on Thursday after a record IPO raise. But the broader market weakened as the high-profile debut did little to ease concerns about the returns on massive AI spending.

"There's definitely a reassessment of AI and some nervousness around the trade," said Mark Preskett, senior portfolio manager at Morningstar Wealth in London. "Investors are sitting on good profits, so there's clearly some profit-taking. Multiples continue to fall for the hyperscalers and especially for semiconductor stocks."

Chip-linked stocks such as ASML , ASM International and STMicroelectronics shed more than 5%, dragging the tech sector (.SX8P) down 3.7% to its lowest level since May.

Among other movers, Vallourec tumbled 12.8% after the French steel pipe maker reported a 26% drop in third-quarter core profit, citing the impact of the Iran conflict and operational disruptions in the United States.

French videogame maker Ubisoft dropped 11.6% after reporting second-quarter net bookings below expectations and issuing a weaker-than-estimated outlook for the current quarter.

Consumer staples stocks outperformed, with Nestle , Unilever and British American Tobacco up more than 1% each as investor sought shelter in defensive sectors.

Despite this week's losses, the STOXX 600 is up 6.2% year-to-date, outperforming the S&P 500's roughly 4.9% gain and underscoring the resilience of European equities, which recently hit record highs on the back of stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings.

Meanwhile, investors await flash eurozone consumer confidence data due later in the day for clues on the region's economic outlook.

data.title: German Recovery Gathers Pace But Lacks Private Investment — Market Talk
data.description: Germany's economy is showing signs of recovery after three years of stagnation, expanding 1% in the first three quarters of 2026, analysts at Berenberg say in a note. Fiscal stimulus, stronger exports and a weaker euro have helped offset high energy costs, while improving sentiment points to further growth as energy prices ease next year. The government's spending package is already boosting public investment, particularly in defense, and growth could accelerate to 1.6% in 2028, they say. But the recovery remains uneven. "Private investment has declined since 2019," the analysts say, highlighting the need for deeper supply-side reforms. Improving conditions for businesses will require progress on pension, healthcare and elderly-care reforms to revive private investment and deliver a more sustainable economic recovery. (don.forbes@wsj.com)

data.title: Top UN Court Finds Myanmar Guilty Of Genocide Against Rohingya
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - The International Court of Justice has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority during military operations in Rakhine State in the last decade. It is the first time the UN's top court has found a state responsible for genocide under the 1948 Genocide Convention.

At the end of a three-hour ruling at the International Court of Justice in The Hague, President Yuji Iwasawa also declared that Myanmar had failed to prevent and punish genocide, after detailing how the eastern Asian country's military had perpetrated 'extreme violence' against mainly Muslim Rohingya communities in Rakhine state.

The ruling establishes that Myanmar's security forces and other State organs intentionally committed specifically prohibited acts covered by Article II of the Genocide Convention.

The ICJ ruling came after studying graphic evidence and testimonies provided by survivors and reports from international investigators describing how Rohingya villages and bridges had been set alight and bulldozed, with men and boys executed and girls and women raped during military clearance operations in northern Rakhine in 2017.

The military clearance operations also involved the murder of infants, which 'supports the inference that Myanmar's security forces acted with the intent to prevent births among the group,' Judge Iwasawa added.

Delivering the court's ruling, the ICJ President described how the mainly Muslim Rohingya living in Rakhine state in western Myanmar had been the target of successive clearance operations by the State military, after decades of intercommunal violence.

The 2017 clearance operations prompted widespread international condemnation after some 700,000 Rohingya fled northern Rakhine state across the border to Bangladesh.

According to the court, an estimated 10,000 Rohingya were killed during the clearance operations, citing supporting evidence.

A separate study estimated that the military and the local Rakhine population killed at least 25,000 Rohingya people.

The case at the ICJ was initiated by The Gambia in November 2019. It has become one of the most closely watched proceedings before the world's highest court.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority in western Myanmar's Rakhine State, were stripped of citizenship under the 1982 Citizenship Law and have faced decades of state discrimination, movement restrictions, and abuse.

More than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh during the 2017 crisis, adding to roughly one million Rohingya refugees living in Bangladeshi camps.

Since 2024, fighting in Rakhine State involving Myanmar's military and the Arakan Army has continued to endanger Rohingya civilians.

The court heard that nearly 400 villages - approximately 40 per cent of the almost 1,000 villages in the three townships of northern Rakhine state - were partially or totally destroyed during and after the 2017 clearance operations.

Myanmar's authorities have consistently denied committing genocide, arguing that military 'clearance operations' were counterterrorism actions responding to attacks by armed groups such as the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The ICJ rejected that defense, finding that the military failed to distinguish between militants and civilians

The Court ordered the government of Myanmar to enact legislation giving full effect to its obligations under the Genocide Convention; to take immediate steps to investigate all persons suspected of having committed acts contrary to the Convention and, if warranted, to prosecute and punish them.

In addition, the ruling orders Myanmar to provide guarantee that such violence is not repeated in the future.

Finally, the Court decided that Myanmar should transmit to it within two years a report on the measures of restitution it has adopted and the amount and modalities of compensation.

The judgment is binding on the parties to the case and without appeal.

UN leadership, human rights organizations, and several governments welcomed the judgment as a milestone for accountability.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres welcomed the judgment as a 'powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide. It is a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand.'

data.title: Asia spot prices fall to 6-week low on weak demand, improved supplies
data.description:
By Emily Chow

Asia spot liquefied natural gas prices slipped for a third consecutive week, weighed down by weaker demand and comfortable inventories in Asia, and improved supplies from the Strait of Hormuz and the US.

The average price for January delivery into northeast Asia (LNG-AS) was estimated at $26.90 per million British thermal units (mmBtu) this week, down from $31.30/mmBtu the previous week and the lowest since October 9.

Continued LNG flows through the Strait of Hormuz and comfortable Asian inventories that limit spot buying interest are easing market pressures, said Ole Dramdal, senior analyst at Rystad Energy.

Some buying interest, however, was visible in South and Southeast Asia, he said, with Thailand, Pakistan and Vietnam showing buying interest.

In northeast Asia, buyers have stepped back from the spot market, with Chinese firms purchasing only enough to meet storage targets, South Korean buyers already covered for winter, and Japanese demand well supplied by long-term contracts, said Martin Senior, head of LNG pricing at Argus.

"And at least four cargoes have diverted away from Egypt this week, prompting further immediate supply availability," he added.

"Egyptian demand has fallen as the nation has cut some fertiliser and industrial supply, and has increased fuel oil imports to replace some gas in power generation."

In Europe, S&P Global Commodity Insights assessed its daily Northwest Europe LNG price benchmark for cargoes delivered in December on an ex-ship basis at $26.765/mmBtu on Thursday, a discount of $0.53/mmBtu to the price at the Dutch TTF gas hub.

Spark Commodities assessed it at $26.572/mmBtu, while Argus assessed the January price at $26.65/mmBtu.

"European LNG prices declined sharply over the week as improving global supply expectations and weak Asian competition outweighed tightening European winter fundamentals," said Aly Blakeway, head of Atlantic LNG at S&P Global Energy, adding that US feedgas around record-high levels pointed to strong Atlantic Basin export availability.

"Middle Eastern supply also continued its gradual recovery. Qatar and Abu Dhabi exported around a cargo per day during the first half of November."

European gas markets, however, remain tight heading into year-end, with low storage levels leaving limited room to absorb additional shocks, said Hans van Cleef, head of energy research at EqoLibrium.

"Weather is the main short-term swing factor; an early cold spell would accelerate withdrawals and create chaos. The issues around the Strait of Hormuz remains the key geopolitical supply risk."

In LNG freight, Atlantic rates fell to $20,500 a day, while Pacific rates declined to $52,000 a day, said Spark Commodities analyst Qasim Afghan.

The US front-month arbitrage to northeast Asia via the Cape of Good Hope continues to point firmly to Europe, while the Nigerian prompt arbitrage, also via the Cape, is pointing to Europe for a fourth straight week, he added.

data.title: Hannover Re Will Try to Reassure Investors Against Volatile Backdrop — Market Talk
data.description: Hannover Re is likely to try to convey the stability of the company at next week's investor day despite the backdrop of sustained price softening in the sector, Berenberg's Michael Christodoulou writes in a note. "This is central to Hannover Re's value proposition, which we think lies in its ability to turn an inherently volatile business into stable earnings growth," the analyst says. The German reinsurer should be able to continue to deliver for shareholders, given its resilience reserve, rising reinvestment yields and a modestly increasing contribution from life and health reinsurance, according to Berenberg. The shares trade at a modest discount to the sector, despite a recent rally, and there is around 15% upside to the current stock price, the analyst says. Shares are up 1.1%. (michael.hennessey@wsj.com)
